name: MCP4822-E_SN
title: MCP4802/4812/4822: dual 8-, 10- and 12-bit voltage-output DACs with internal 2.048 V reference and SPI
summary: Dual buffered voltage-output DACs, 8-bit (MCP4802), 10-bit (MCP4812) and 12-bit (MCP4822), with an internal 2.048 V reference and a selectable 1x or 2x output gain for a 2.048 V or 4.096 V full scale. They run from one 2.7 V to 5.5 V supply, take 16-bit write commands over SPI at up to 20 MHz, update both outputs together through LDAC and can shut each channel down. Specified from -40 °C to +125 °C in MSOP-8, PDIP-8 and SOIC-8; MCP4822-E/SN is the 12-bit part in SOIC-8.
key_figures: 2.7 V to 5.5 V; IDD 415 µA typ, 750 µA max at 5 V

pins.name: VDD
pins.function: Positive supply, 2.7V to 5.5V referred to VSS. Bypass with about 0.1 µF ceramic to ground, with a 10 µF tantalum in parallel for high-frequency noise on the board.

pins.name: CS
pins.function: Chip select, active low: low enables the serial clock and data inputs.

pins.name: LDAC
pins.function: Latch DAC input, active low. Low moves both input registers into the output registers so VOUTA and VOUTB change together. Held at VSS, each output updates on the rising edge of CS; it may also be driven from an MCU I/O.

pins.name: VOUTB
pins.function: DAC B output, from its own amplifier; range VSS to G × VREF, never above VDD.

pins.name: VSS
pins.function: Analog ground and current return for all circuits in the device. Connect to a ground plane by a low-impedance path, on the analog ground where the board has one.

pins.name: VOUTA
pins.function: DAC A output, from its own amplifier; range VSS to G × VREF, never above VDD.

circuits.title: Typical connection diagram
circuits.description: Two dual DACs share one microcontroller SPI port: SDO, SCK and LDAC run to both, and each DAC has its own chip select (CS0 to U1, CS1 to U2), so pulling LDAC low updates all four outputs at once. Every supply pin, the DACs and the MCU alike, is bypassed by 10 µF and 0.1 µF in parallel to ground, and each VOUTA carries 1 µF to ground. The VOUTB outputs are optional.
notes: The DAC grounds are analog ground (AVSS); the MCU ground is VSS.
C1 to C6 sit within 4 mm of the VDD pins they serve.

circuits.title: Set point or threshold calibration
circuits.description: A photodiode from VDD into RSENSE makes a light-dependent voltage at the comparator inverting input. The DAC output, scaled down by the R1/R2 divider and filtered by 0.1 µF, sets the trip voltage VTRIP at the non-inverting input; a smaller divided range gives finer steps per code. Any of the single or dual 8-, 10- or 12-bit parts fits the DAC position.
notes: The SPI link uses three lines (CS, SCK, SDI); with three lines LDAC sits at VSS and the output updates on the rising edge of CS.
On a dual part either channel serves; the other output is unused.

circuits.title: Single-supply window DAC
circuits.description: The set-point circuit with a pull-up R3 to VCC+ and a pull-down R2 to VCC– at the trip node. Their Thevenin equivalent V23 through R23 and the DAC through R1 together set VTRIP, so the full code range spans a narrow window around the wanted threshold and each step is smaller. The sensor and RSENSE form a divider whose midpoint feeds the comparator inverting input.
notes: The SPI link uses three lines (CS, SCK, SDI); with three lines LDAC sits at VSS and the output updates on the rising edge of CS.
The sensor's upper terminal goes to an unnamed supply.

circuits.title: Digitally-controlled bipolar voltage source
circuits.description: An external op amp turns the 0 to 4.096 V DAC output into a bipolar one. R3 and R4 divide VOUT to VIN+ (filtered by 0.1 µF); R1 from VDD and R2 in feedback set the gain and pull the output negative, so VO = VIN+ (1 + R2/R1) – VDD (R2/R1). With R1 = 20 kΩ, R2 = 10 kΩ, R3 = 10 kΩ and R4 = 20 kΩ, a 12-bit part at G = 2 covers ±2.05 V in about 1 mV steps.

parts.note: from VDD to the inverting input

notes: The SPI link uses three lines (CS, SCK, SDI); with three lines LDAC sits at VSS and the output updates on the rising edge of CS.
R1 to R4 are the worked-design values for ±2.05 V in 1 mV steps.
R4 may go to VDD instead of VSS for a higher offset, or a pull-up to VDD may replace or join R4.

circuits.title: Bipolar voltage source with selectable gain and offset
circuits.description: Both channels of one dual DAC drive an external op amp. DACA through R1 into the inverting node sets the gain term; DACB through R3 into the non-inverting node, with R4 to VCC–, sets the offset; R2 is the feedback resistor and 0.1 µF filters VIN+. Fitting R5 from VIN+ to VCC+ makes a bipolar window version whose range narrows around a chosen centre. Used to linearize a sensor whose slope and offset both vary.

parts.note: VIN+ to VCC+; optional, fitted for the window version

notes: The SPI link uses three lines; LDAC sits at VSS and each output updates on the rising edge of CS.
Works from a bipolar or a single supply; MCP4802, MCP4812 or MCP4822.

circuits.title: Simple double-precision DAC with MCP4822
circuits.description: The two outputs of one MCP4822 are summed by a divider, R1 from VOUTA and R2 from VOUTB with R1 much larger than R2, and buffered by an op amp follower; 0.1 µF filters the summing node. VOUTB sets the coarse level in 1 mV steps and VOUTA, attenuated about 1000 times, trims it in about 1 µV steps, up to 22-bit resolution over 0 to 4.1 V. With R2 = 100 Ω, R1 = 100 kΩ.
notes: The SPI link uses three lines (CS, SCK, SDI); with three lines LDAC sits at VSS and the output updates on the rising edge of CS.
R1 and R2 are the worked-design values for 1 µV steps over 0 V to 4.1 V; the general condition is R1 >> R2.

circuits.title: Digitally-controlled current source
circuits.description: An op amp follower drives the base of an NPN transistor whose emitter returns through RSENSE to ground and to the op amp inverting input, so the DAC voltage appears across RSENSE and sets the load current IL drawn from VDD or VREF through the load at the collector. A capacitor on VOUT filters the DAC output. A smaller RSENSE wastes less power; the window divider of the window DAC can narrow the range for finer current steps.
notes: The SPI link uses three lines (CS, SCK, SDI); with three lines LDAC sits at VSS and the output updates on the rising edge of CS.
On a dual part either channel serves; the other output is unused.

operation.text: MCP4802, MCP4812 and MCP4822 are the 8-, 10- and 12-bit members of one dual voltage-output DAC family with an internal 2.048 V reference, rail-to-rail buffered outputs and an SPI input, in 8-pin PDIP, SOIC and MSOP. Single-channel versions are MCP4801/4811/4821; MCP4901/4911/4921 (single) and MCP4902/4912/4922 (dual) take an external reference. These relatives have similar AC and DC performance.

Each channel is a resistor-string DAC fed from its own input register and DAC register, followed by gain logic and an output op amp. The interface logic takes CS, SDI, SCK and LDAC; a power-on reset circuit watches VDD. The string architecture gives low DNL, a low ratiometric temperature coefficient and fast settling.
The GA bit sets the output amplifier gain: GA = 1 gives 1x (0 to 2.048 V full scale), GA = 0 gives 2x (0 to 4.096 V). The power-up default is GA = 0, gain 2. The output can never exceed VDD.

Each output is a low-power precision CMOS amplifier with low offset and low noise whose output stage swings close to both rails. It drives resistive loads and large capacitive loads without oscillating, strongly enough for VOUT to serve as a programmable reference; most applications need no external buffer.
Both channels use the internal 2.048 V reference, whose drift with temperature and whose noise are both low. Shutting a channel down leaves the reference running.

Below the POR threshold (VPOR = 2.0 V typical) both DACs are held in reset. At power-up the outputs come up in shutdown, high impedance (about 500 kΩ), and stay there until VDD is above VPOR, a valid write command has been received and LDAC is below its input low threshold. A dip of VDD below VPOR resets the part only when its depth and duration together lie above the typical transient-response boundary. A 0.1 µF decoupling capacitor as close as possible to VDD adds immunity to such transients.

Writing SHDN = 0 shuts down the addressed channel: most of its circuits turn off, the output amplifier stops driving and VOUT is switched to a 500 kΩ (typical) resistive load. The reference and the serial interface stay active, so a later write with SHDN = 1 brings the channel back. Leaving shutdown, the output settles in under 10 µs, longer than the 4.5 µs of a normal active-mode change.

SPI, modes 0,0 and 1,1, write only: nothing can be read back. Data enters on SDI on the rising edge of SCK, MSb first, while CS is held low for the whole command. A command is one 16-bit word, four configuration bits and twelve data bits; clocks after the 16th are ignored. Raising CS after 16 clocks latches the word into the addressed input register; raising CS before 16 clocks aborts the transfer, and nothing is accepted while CS is high. The link also suits Microwire peripherals.

The registers are double-buffered. Driving LDAC low copies both input registers into the DAC registers so VOUTA and VOUTB change together. With LDAC tied to VSS the interface needs three I/O lines instead of four and each output updates as soon as a valid 16-clock word ends with CS rising.

INL is the largest deviation of an actual code transition from its ideal position once offset and gain errors are removed, measured by the end-point method from 0x000 to 0xFFF. Positive INL is a transition later than ideal, negative earlier.

DNL is how far each code width differs from the ideal 1 LSb; zero DNL means every code is exactly 1 LSb wide. Offset error is the output at code zero. Gain error is the departure of the full-scale output from its ideal of VREF – 1 LSb, offset error excluded.

VDD runs from 2.7 V to 5.5 V and should be as clean as possible. Use two bypass capacitors in parallel, 0.1 µF ceramic and 10 µF tantalum, within 4 mm of the VDD pin; they suppress noise from digital switching and from changes of the DAC output. Where the board has separate analog and digital supplies, VDD and VSS belong on the analog plane.

Output noise comes mainly from the internal reference, with a 1/f corner near 400 Hz. A small capacitor on VOUT forms a single-pole low-pass filter: sized for a 1 kHz corner it brings ENREF to about 100 µVrms, which is needed to reach the low DNL the parts can achieve at G = 1. Output capacitance from 0.001 µF to 4.7 µF has been tested stable.

Inductively coupled transients and digital switching noise degrade the output. Best results come from a multilayer board: a ground plane of low inductance, inputs and outputs kept apart from each other, and good decoupling; harsh environments may need shielded signals. Breadboards and wire-wrap are unsuitable where low noise matters.

The MCP4822 has 4096 steps: 500 µV each at G = 1 and 1 mV at G = 2. For a narrower range with finer steps, such as a 0.8 V bias range at about 200 µV per step, either lower the reference (an MCP49xx part with an external 0.82 V reference) or divide the DAC output with two resistors. A low reference can bring an unacceptable noise floor; the divider keeps a larger reference and also suits ranges no reference gives. A bypass capacitor on the divider output removes DAC and pickup noise.

Setting a sensor threshold usually uses only a small part of the output range. When the LSb is too coarse and the threshold lies away from VSS, VREF and 2VREF, a pull-up and pull-down at the divider node centre a narrow window on the threshold, raising the resolution there.

Target: ±2.05 V in 1 mV steps. The range is 4.1 V, needing 4100 steps, so 12 bits (4096) suffice. Choose G = 2 (4.096 V full scale) and set code 0 to give –2.05 V: R2/R1 = 1/2, met by R1 = 20 kΩ and R2 = 10 kΩ. Then set full scale to give +2.05 V: R4/(R3 + R4) = 2/3, met by R4 = 20 kΩ and R3 = 10 kΩ. A higher offset is had by returning R4 to VDD, or adding a pull-up to VDD.

Target: 1 µV steps over 0 V to 4.1 V, about 4.1 × 10^6 steps, which is 22 bits. DACB alone gives 1 mV steps; since its DNL is ±0.75 LSb, DACA scaled down 1000 times can fill in and correct between them. R2 = 100 Ω with R1 = 100 kΩ gives that ratio. Up to 24-bit resolution is possible this way from one MCP4822.

With an op amp and transistor around RSENSE, the DAC voltage sets a load current. A smaller RSENSE dissipates less power but also coarsens current control; adding the window divider narrows the range for finer steps. With very small sensor voltages, cancel the amplifier offset by storing the DAC setting found under known sensor conditions.
This family runs on the Mixed Signal PICtail Demo Board.
